title: The Nanaksar tradition
hookLine: a tradition of continuous kirtan and reading begun by Baba Nand Singh

lines: A BATON THAT NEVER TOUCHES THE GROUND.
ONE READER HANDS ON TO THE NEXT.
cards: A relay race only works if the baton never touches the ground. One runner tires, and another is already moving alongside, hand out. Now set that race indoors, slow it down, and make the baton a voice.

One reader finishes a stretch of the Guru Granth Sahib, and another is already seated, ready to go on without a gap. Down the hall, a small group sings, and when they rest, another group takes up the hymn.
That is the picture at a Nanaksar gurdwara: the praise doesn't stop when one person does.

teach.h: BABA NAND SINGH: MEDITATION AND REVERENCE.
teach.b: The Nanaksar tradition grew around Baba Nand Singh, a holy man remembered for long stretches of solitary meditation and a deep, almost personal reverence for the Guru Granth Sahib.
His followers carried on what he began, and Nanaksar centers keep it going today. Three things stand out.

teach.h: READING AND KIRTAN KEPT GOING IN TURNS.
teach.b: First, continuous praise: reading of the Granth and singing of kirtan are kept going in turns, so the Guru's word is always sounding somewhere in the house.

teach.h: THE GRANTH HONORED AS A LIVING GURU.
teach.b: Second, the Granth treated as a living Guru in very concrete ways.
Nanaksar is known for care like that given to an honored person: food prepared and offered with great attention, the Granth's resting place kept with tenderness.
The Granth is Guru for the whole panth; Nanaksar is known for making that honor detailed and constant.
Third, simplicity of life for those who lead: tradition remembers the babas of Nanaksar as renunciants who asked little for themselves. Where does continuous praise come from?
Open the Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan's long hymn of peace, on Ang 262.
Its first stanza opens, in paraphrase: remember, remember, keep remembering, and find peace. The repetition is the teaching.
Simran, the word for remembering, isn't a single act; the hymn says it over and over, as if to show it should never quite stop. A Nanaksar center turns that line into the shape of a building.
Sikhs hold different views about some Nanaksar customs and their place beside the common code.
The aim itself is plain: a house where the praise doesn't fall silent.

how: At Nanaksar centers, readers and kirtan singers take turns so that the Guru Granth Sahib's words are kept sounding continuously, and the Granth is served with detailed care as a living Guru.

o: a school that copies the Granth out by hand
a stream keeping the Guru's word always sounding
an order of riders that guards the Granth

s: only Nanaksar Sikhs honor the Granth as Guru
the Granth is Guru for the whole panth; Nanaksar is known for making that honor detailed and constant.
the Sukhmani Sahib's first stanza repeats the call to remember
remember, remember, keep remembering, and find peace.
at Nanaksar the reading stops whenever one reader tires
another reader is ready, so the praise goes on in turns.

games.q: you're reading the Granth at a Nanaksar center and your stretch is ending. what happens next?
o: the room waits in silence until morning.
another reader is already seated to go on without a gap.
the reading starts again from the beginning.
games.why: the reading is handed on, like a relay, so the Guru's word keeps sounding.

practice: Play a recording of Gurbani kirtan low enough that you have to lean in, or listen to the quietest sound in the room. When your attention drifts, come back, the way one reader hands on to the next; each return is a fresh start.
If you pray, rest on Waheguru as you return.
